t.5.54.1: Then, saluting Jānakī, who was standing at the foot of the śiṃśapā tree, he said: "By good fortune I see you here unharmed."
t.5.54.2: Then Sītā, gazing again and again at Hanūmān as he set out, spoke to him words filled with love for her husband.
t.5.54.4: But if Kākutstha, the crusher of enemy forces, should fill Laṅkā with his armies and lead me away, that would be worthy of him.
t.5.54.3: Indeed, you alone are fully capable of accomplishing this task, O slayer of enemy heroes; this surge of your strength brings you glory.
t.5.54.6: Having heard her words, full of meaning, courteous and grounded in reason, Hanumān spoke these words in reply.
t.5.54.5: You yourself must bring that about, so that the valor of that great-souled one, a hero in battle, may prove worthy of him.
t.5.54.7: Soon Kākutstha will come, surrounded by the foremost of the monkeys and bears, he who, having conquered his enemies in battle, will dispel your sorrow.
t.5.54.8: Having thus comforted Vaidehī, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, set his mind on departing and respectfully saluted Vaidehī.
t.5.54.9: Then that tiger among monkeys, the crusher of foes, eager to behold his master, ascended Ariṣṭa, the best of mountains.
t.5.54.10: It was encircled by dark-blue stretches of forest thronged with tuṅga and padmaka trees, and by many sāla, tāla and aśvakarṇa trees and bamboos.
t.5.54.11: It was adorned with wide-spread canopies of flowering creepers, crowded with herds of many kinds of beasts, and embellished with streams trickling from its mineral ores.
t.5.54.12: the mountain abounding in many springs, crowded with masses of rock, and frequented by great sages, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras and serpents.
t.5.54.13: The mountain thick with creepers and trees, its caves teeming with lions, thronged with packs of tigers, and full of trees bearing sweet roots and fruits.
t.5.54.14: That exceedingly mighty best of monkeys climbed the mountain, spurred on by a joy that made him hasten to see Rāma.
t.5.54.15: On the lovely mountain ridges, the rocks trodden by the soles of his feet shattered with a roar and were then ground to powder.
t.5.54.16: Having ascended that lord of mountains, the great monkey expanded his body, longing to reach the northern shore of the salt ocean from the southern.
t.5.54.17: Then the heroic son of the Wind, having climbed the mountain, beheld the fearsome ocean, frequented by fish and serpents.
t.5.54.18: Like the wind itself, that tiger among monkeys, the son born of Māruta, took to the sky and made his way from the south toward the northern quarter.
t.5.54.19: Then that best of mountains, crushed by that monkey, roared together with those beings and sank into the surface of the earth, with its peaks quaking and its trees falling.
t.5.54.20: Churned by the force of his thighs, the trees rich with blossoms fell broken to the ground, as if struck down by Śakra's weapon.
t.5.54.21: The terrible roar of the mighty lions dwelling in the hollows of the caves, crushed and afflicted, was heard, as if splitting the sky.
t.5.54.22: Their garments slipping and disarrayed, their ornaments thrown into disorder, the Vidyādharīs suddenly flew up from the mountain.
t.5.54.24: Likewise the Kiṃnaras, Uragas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas and Vidyādharas, abandoning that oppressed best of mountains, took their stand in the sky.
t.5.54.23: The great serpents, enormous in size and mighty, with flaming tongues and deadly venom, writhed about, their heads and necks crushed.
t.5.54.25: And that splendid mountain, pressed down by that mighty one, sank into Rasātala together with its trees and its lofty peaks.
t.5.54.26: That mountain, ten yojanas in breadth and rising thirty yojanas high, was brought level with the earth.
